classification.difficultyReason: Classify familiar exact numbers and convert rational values to simplest fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses rational versus irrational classification; fractions are required only for rational values.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a rational number as an integer ratio, convert mixed numbers and decimals to fractions, simplify by common factors, and recognise irrational roots and pi.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Classify familiar exact numbers and convert rational values to simplest fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate direct verbal descriptions into endpoint inequalities.

questions.mappingNote: Each verbal interval translates directly into inequalities.
questions.methodNote: Use strict inequality signs for excluded endpoints and inclusive signs for included endpoints.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate direct verbal descriptions into endpoint inequalities.

classification.difficultyReason: Select brackets for included and excluded endpoints, including unbounded intervals.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess verbal-to-bracket interval conversion.
questions.methodNote: Write endpoints in increasing order, using square brackets for inclusion and round brackets for exclusion and infinity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select brackets for included and excluded endpoints, including unbounded intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Graph inequalities using endpoint inclusion and ray direction.

questions.mappingNote: Each inequality is represented as an interval on a real number line.
questions.methodNote: Use open circles for excluded endpoints, closed circles for included endpoints, and arrows for unbounded intervals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Graph inequalities using endpoint inclusion and ray direction.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert bracket intervals into number-line graphs with appropriate endpoints and rays.

questions.mappingNote: Each bracket interval requires a number-line graph.
questions.methodNote: Interpret square and round brackets as included and excluded endpoints; show unbounded intervals using arrows.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert bracket intervals into number-line graphs with appropriate endpoints and rays.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate strict and inclusive inequalities into bounded and unbounded interval notation.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess inequality-to-interval conversion.
questions.methodNote: Use square brackets for inclusive inequalities, round brackets for strict inequalities, and round brackets at infinity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate strict and inclusive inequalities into bounded and unbounded interval notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate bracket inclusion directly into inequality signs.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts reverse the bracket-notation examples taught on these pages.
questions.methodNote: Square brackets include endpoints; round brackets exclude endpoints. Infinite bounds use round brackets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate bracket inclusion directly into inequality signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Bound square and cube roots using neighbouring perfect powers without a calculator.

questions.mappingNote: Root bounds follow the number-line treatment of irrational numbers; page 4 supplies the approximation to pi.
questions.methodNote: Locate irrational real numbers between integers; use integer powers and the familiar approximation to pi.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Bound square and cube roots using neighbouring perfect powers without a calculator.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied definitions separately to endpoint inclusion and extension indefinitely; no inference between the two classifications is required.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 explicitly classifies single-ended rays as open or closed and unbounded.
questions.methodNote: Classify intervals by inclusion of their finite endpoints and by whether they extend indefinitely.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied definitions separately to endpoint inclusion and extension indefinitely; no inference between the two classifications is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify primes and apply familiar prime factorisation, including expressing a power of ten using prime powers..

questions.mappingNote: The complete printed prime-list prefix from page 2 is embedded in part a so the task is self-contained.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of primes and unique decomposition of composite whole numbers into prime factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify primes and apply familiar prime factorisation, including expressing a power of ten using prime powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Include negative integer factors and construct products with distinct signed factors.

questions.mappingNote: These tasks apply the whole-number factor discussion and extension to integers.
questions.methodNote: Use integer factors, including negative integers, and the sign rules for integer multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Include negative integer factors and construct products with distinct signed factors; closest supplied skill is rational-numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerate distinct rational values under denominator and interval restrictions, then find an LCM.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines the rational-number definition with a closed interval and the known magnitude of pi; part b directly applies page 3's LCM method.
questions.methodNote: Represent rationals with integer numerators and nonzero integer denominators; use the LCM for a common denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Enumerate distinct rational values under denominator and interval restrictions, then find an LCM.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret or as a union and and as an intersection before simplifying the interval.

questions.mappingNote: The logical conditions simplify to the whole real line or one closed interval using the taught bracket notation.
questions.methodNote: Describe connected sets on the real line using included or excluded endpoints and infinite bounds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret or as a union and and as an intersection before simplifying the interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the fully supplied contradiction proof to sqrt(3), establishing its nonintegrality and carrying over the reduced-denominator argument.

questions.mappingNote: The worked answer follows the actual page 4 proof, rather than substituting the alternative divisibility-by-three proof. Its supplied sqrt(2) argument is embedded as permanent question context.
questions.methodNote: Use contradiction: a reduced fraction remains reduced after squaring, so a nontrivial denominator cannot yield an integer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Adapt the fully supplied contradiction proof to sqrt(3), establishing its nonintegrality and carrying over the reduced-denominator argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the positive square roots of eight perfect squares.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates the principal square root of a perfect square, directly applying the definition and basic square-root result rather than collecting or simplifying irrational surds.
questions.methodNote: Printed page 33 defines the square-root symbol as the positive square root and illustrates this with square root of 25 equal to 5. Printed page 34 restates the square-root laws.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recall the positive square roots of eight perfect squares.

classification.difficultyReason: Each part requires extracting a perfect-square factor from one square root.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses simplifying a single surd by extracting square factors; no collection of terms or rationalisation is required. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: Use the product law for nonnegative square roots, take out a square divisor and continue until the radicand has no square divisor other than 1, as in Laws concerning surds, Simplifying a surd and Example 1 on PDF page 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Each part requires extracting a perfect-square factor from one square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like surds, retaining unlike surds and handling negative coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses addition or subtraction of like surds. Parts a–d have one radicand; parts e–i require collecting two distinct radicands separately. This directly matches simplify-surds-operations.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 defines surds and positive square roots. Page 9 Example 2 collects like surds after simplification; unlike surds remain separate. These parts already have simplified radicands, so collect their signed coefficients directly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like surds, retaining unlike surds and handling negative coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract a perfect-square factor from each radicand and multiply its square root by the supplied coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses simplifying a coefficient times a square root: a uses 8=4×2; b uses 12=4×3; c uses 24=4×6; d uses 44=4×11; e uses 45=9×5; f uses 52=4×13; g uses 300=100×3; h uses 96=16×6. No whole-question reuse candidate matches these eight givens.
questions.methodNote: Use the square-root product law, take out perfect-square divisors, and multiply by the existing coefficient, following Laws concerning surds, Simplifying a surd and Example 1 on PDF page 9. Retain the irrational factor throughout.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract a perfect-square factor from each radicand and multiply its square root by the supplied coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Express a positive integer coefficient as its square root and combine two square roots using the product law.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the basic surd product result in reverse; no collection, expansion or rationalisation is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Use the positive-square-root definition on PDF page 8 and the square-root product law in Laws concerning surds on PDF page 9. Follow the demonstration embedded in Question 5: replace the positive coefficient by the square root of its square, then combine the roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express a positive integer coefficient as its square root and combine two square roots using the product law.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract square factors and collect like surds in parts a–i; recognise exact higher roots in parts j–l.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e simplify two square roots and collect like terms. Parts f–i apply the same method to three terms. Parts j–l evaluate exact higher roots. The whole question primarily assesses simplification of surd expressions, with basic root results supporting the final three parts.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 defines positive square roots, cube roots and higher-root notation. Page 9 gives the product law, extraction of square divisors and collection of like surds in Examples 1–2. Extract square factors before collecting coefficients; evaluate higher roots using their defining powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract square factors and collect like surds in parts a–i; recognise exact higher roots in parts j–l.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract square factors from three terms, apply coefficients and subtraction signs, then collect like surds while retaining unlike terms.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires simplifying square roots before collecting like terms. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and givens, so neither is source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Use the square-root product law and extract square divisors as in page 9 Example 1, then collect like surds as in Example 2. Retain unlike surds separately. Independently correct the dropped square-root factor in Example 1(b) when applying its method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract square factors from three terms, apply coefficients and subtraction signs, then collect like surds while retaining unlike terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract square factors and collect like surds, then square the resulting nonnegative expression to determine x.

questions.mappingNote: Part a reduces to sqrt(7); part b to 2sqrt(5); part c to 4sqrt(6); and part d to 2sqrt(6). Each part directly assesses surd simplification followed by the square-root identity.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 defines the positive square root. Page 9 gives the square-root laws, extraction of square divisors and collection of like surds in Examples 1 and 2. Simplify each left-hand side, then use the square of the positive square root to recover x.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract square factors and collect like surds, then square the resulting nonnegative expression to determine x.

classification.difficultyReason: Establish strict bounds using perfect powers, then combine three bounds to prove the required inequality without numerical approximation.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply root results to exact inequalities; part b combines square-, cube- and fourth-root bounds. Neither supplied reuse candidate is the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 defines the positive square root and explains cube roots and higher roots. Page 9 recalls basic root laws and perfect squares. Compare positive roots with integer bounds using the corresponding perfect powers, then add the strict inequalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establish strict bounds using perfect powers, then combine three bounds to prove the required inequality without numerical approximation.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect irrational roots with the absence of rational intercepts, while explaining positive and negative function values.

questions.mappingNote: The central explanation depends on recognising that both square roots of 2 are irrational; rational examples establish points above and below the axis.
questions.methodNote: Use the two opposite square roots of a positive number and the irrationality of square roots of non-square rational numbers. Identify an x-intercept by setting y equal to zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect irrational roots with the absence of rational intercepts, while explaining positive and negative function values.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply square-root product and squaring identities, multiplying numerical coefficients where present.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess basic surd products or squares; no binomial expansion is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the product identity sqrt(a) × sqrt(b) = sqrt(ab), multiply coefficients separately, and simplify square roots of perfect squares, following Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square-root product and squaring identities, multiplying numerical coefficients where present.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide numerical coefficients and positive square roots, treating each following surd monomial as the complete divisor.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess division of surd expressions. In f–h, the complete following monomial is the divisor, as confirmed independently by the answer key.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 uses the product identity for square roots, separates numerical factors and simplifies radicals in Example 3. These divisions use the corresponding quotient rule and cancellation of numerical coefficients; no quotient demonstration is printed on the supplied teaching page.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide numerical coefficients and positive square roots, treating each following surd monomial as the complete divisor.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute one surd monomial across a binomial and simplify square-root products.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts require expanding a surd monomial times a binomial; simplification of the resulting products is part of the same assessed method.
questions.methodNote: Use distribution as demonstrated in Example 4(a), multiply radicals using the product identity, and simplify perfect-square factors as in Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distribute one surd monomial across a binomial and simplify square-root products.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply surds and numerical coefficients, then extract square factors to simplify fully.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess multiplication and full simplification of surds; no binomial expansion is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the product identity for square roots, multiply numerical coefficients, and extract square factors as demonstrated in Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply surds and numerical coefficients, then extract square factors to simplify fully.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute a surd monomial over two terms, multiply radicals and simplify square factors.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts require expansion followed by simplification of radical products, so expand-surd-expressions is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 4(a) distributes multiplication over brackets; Example 3 multiplies surds and extracts square factors. Apply those steps in that order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distribute a surd monomial over two terms, multiply radicals and simplify square factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand two binomials, simplify radical products and collect like terms, including signed coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess expansion of surd binomials. Parts a–c retain unlike radicals; parts d–f also combine like radical terms. The supplied reuse candidates do not contain this complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 distributes each term across the second binomial, simplifies radical products using square factors, and collects like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand two binomials, simplify radical products and collect like terms, including signed coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise conjugate factors and apply the supplied difference-of-squares identity, including squared surd coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess expansion of conjugate surd binomials. The supplied special expansion is retained in the shared instruction.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 teaches multiplication of surds and expansion of surd binomials using algebraic identities. Question 7 supplies the difference-of-squares identity explicitly; substitute each pair of terms, square the complete terms and simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise conjugate factors and apply the supplied difference-of-squares identity, including squared surd coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied square identities, including coefficients on surds, and simplify the resulting products and square factors.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess expansion of surd binomials using the supplied identities; part i additionally requires simplifying sqrt(50).
questions.methodNote: Example 4b applies the square-of-a-difference identity, evaluates squared surds, combines integer terms and extracts a square factor from the remaining radical. Question 8 supplies both square identities explicitly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied square identities, including coefficients on surds, and simplify the resulting products and square factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine products and quotients of radicals, simplify square factors and cancel numerical coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess simplifying products and quotients of surds. No binomial expansion or conjugate denominator is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the product identity and extract square factors as demonstrated in Example 3; combine these operations with quotient simplification for the fractional expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine products and quotients of radicals, simplify square factors and cancel numerical coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply Pythagoras’ theorem with exact surd lengths, expanding conjugate binomial squares in parts c and d.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b square single surd terms. Parts c and d require binomial expansion before cancellation, making expansion of surd expressions the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 multiplies surds and simplifies square factors. Example 4 expands surd binomials, including the identity (A−B)²=A²−2AB+B². Apply these operations after the question’s explicit Pythagoras instruction and take the positive square root for a length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply Pythagoras’ theorem with exact surd lengths, expanding conjugate binomial squares in parts c and d.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise square factors and perfect-square trinomials, then simplify radicals using the positive-variable conditions.

questions.mappingNote: The principal assessed skill is applying square-root identities to algebraic square factors; parts c–f additionally require recognising or factoring perfect-square trinomials.
questions.methodNote: Use the product identity for square roots and extract square factors as in Example 3. Recognise the perfect-square expansions illustrated in Example 4. Positivity of x and y makes all extracted factors positive.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise square factors and perfect-square trinomials, then simplify radicals using the positive-variable conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a counterexample, then expand a square and check the sign condition to characterise all cases of equality.

questions.mappingNote: Part a tests the limitation of distributing a square root over a sum. Part b uses binomial expansion to derive the equality conditions; expand-surd-expressions is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 expands binomial products and simplifies surds. Apply the square expansion to the proposed equality, retaining the non-negative value of a square root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a counterexample, then expand a square and check the sign condition to characterise all cases of equality.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare positive surds by squaring; rearrange the differences of compound expressions before making exact comparisons.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require exact comparison using surd operations. Parts c and d additionally require collecting surd terms in a difference. Comparing positive squares extends the supplied surd identities to the enrichment task.
questions.methodNote: Use the product identity for surds and algebraic simplification shown in Examples 3 and 4. For exact comparisons, compare squares of positive quantities; for compound expressions, simplify their difference first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare positive surds by squaring; rearrange the differences of compound expressions before making exact comparisons.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied expansion-and-squaring scaffold, simplify the conjugate product and use positivity to select the square root.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c extend the same binomial-expansion method to nested radicals; the product of the conjugate radicands simplifies exactly before taking the positive square root.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 expands surd binomials and uses the identity (A−B)^2=A^2−2AB+B^2, then simplifies square factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied expansion-and-squaring scaffold, simplify the conjugate product and use positivity to select the square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the sum and difference square identities to determine the sum directly from the given difference and product.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the same binomial square identities to relate the required sum to the supplied difference and product, without solving for either variable.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 expands surd binomials and uses the square identity before simplifying exact radicals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect the sum and difference square identities to determine the sum directly from the given difference and product.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied intermediate identities scaffold the expansion, rearrangement and repeated substitution; the main decision is recognising how to insert part b into part c.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies the taught surd-binomial expansion; parts b and c rearrange and simplify its consequences, and part d extends them through repeated substitution.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 expands surd binomials using distribution and the square identity, then simplifies square roots and collects terms. Parts b–d use the algebraic consequences explicitly scaffolded by this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The supplied intermediate identities scaffold the expansion, rearrangement and repeated substitution; the main decision is recognising how to insert part b into part c.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct recognition of conjugates by changing the sign between two terms.

questions.mappingNote: Identifying conjugates directly assesses the conjugate component of rationalising binomial surd denominators.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 introduces difference of squares for rationalisation. Page 15 defines conjugates as expressions with the same two terms and opposite signs between them.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct recognition of conjugates by changing the sign between two terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the difference-of-squares identity to four supplied conjugate pairs.

questions.mappingNote: The requested result is a product of surd binomials, so expanding and simplifying surd expressions is the primary skill. Identifying conjugates supports the binomial-rationalisation skill.
questions.methodNote: Use conjugates and the difference of squares: (A+B)(A−B)=A²−B². Example 6 and summary 12 square both coefficients and surd terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the difference-of-squares identity to four supplied conjugate pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the same single-term rationalisation procedure to eight fractions, combining radical products where needed.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses rationalising a single-term surd denominator; parts e–h additionally combine radicals in the numerator.
questions.methodNote: Page 14, rule 10 and Example 5: multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's square root, combine radical products and simplify. Page 15's conjugate method is unnecessary for these single-term denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the same single-term rationalisation procedure to eight fractions, combining radical products where needed.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify each denominator's conjugate and apply the explicitly taught difference-of-squares procedure, including squaring surd coefficients; no additional connection is required.

questions.mappingNote: Every part has a two-term denominator. Parts a–f use unit surd coefficients; g–h additionally square the coefficient multiplying the surd.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate, then apply the difference of squares, following Example 6 and summaries 11–12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify each denominator's conjugate and apply the explicitly taught difference-of-squares procedure, including squaring surd coefficients; no additional connection is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the same single-term rationalisation method to eight fractions and reduce the resulting rational coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Every part has a single surd denominator and directly assesses rationalising a single-term denominator; conjugates are unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Key Idea 10 and Example 5 on PDF page 14 multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's surd, evaluate its square and simplify the rational coefficient. Page 15 distinguishes the conjugate method for binomial denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the same single-term rationalisation method to eight fractions and reduce the resulting rational coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's radical, then simplify numerical factors.

questions.mappingNote: All eight fractions have single-term surd denominators, so rationalise-denominator directly matches the assessed method; no conjugates are needed.
questions.methodNote: Key idea 10 and Example 5 on PDF page 14 multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's radical, evaluate its square and simplify. Page 15 distinguishes the conjugate method for binomial denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's radical, then simplify numerical factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Select conjugates, evaluate differences of squares and simplify surd numerators, including squared binomials.

questions.mappingNote: Every part has a binomial surd denominator and directly assesses conjugate-based rationalisation. Parts g–l also require expanding squared surd binomials.
questions.methodNote: Key Idea 11 and Example 6 multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate, then apply the difference of squares. Key Idea 12 defines conjugates. Expand and simplify the resulting numerator, retaining exact surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select conjugates, evaluate differences of squares and simplify surd numerators, including squared binomials.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the conjugate, expand surd binomials and simplify the resulting numerator and rational denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess rationalising a binomial surd denominator with a binomial surd numerator.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate, use the difference of squares in the denominator, then expand and simplify the numerator, following Example 6 and the conjugates summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose the conjugate, expand surd binomials and simplify the resulting numerator and rational denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Rationalise two denominators in each expression and combine the resulting terms to demonstrate cancellation of the surds.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require binomial rationalisation and cancellation across two fractions; parts a and b additionally use single-term rationalisation.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's surd for a single-term denominator, or by its conjugate for a binomial denominator. Apply the difference of squares, then simplify and combine like surds, following Examples 5 and 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rationalise two denominators in each expression and combine the resulting terms to demonstrate cancellation of the surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a given surd value into a reciprocal expression and use its conjugate to prove the stated identity.

questions.mappingNote: The reciprocal has a binomial surd denominator; rationalising it establishes the required identity without introducing another method.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate, then use the difference of squares, as demonstrated in Example 6 and the conjugates explanation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a given surd value into a reciprocal expression and use its conjugate to prove the stated identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the conjugate, expand the numerator, collect like surds and identify two signed coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses rationalising a binomial surd denominator, followed by simplifying the numerator and comparing coefficients with the required form.
questions.methodNote: Use the conjugate to rationalise a two-term denominator, applying the difference of squares as demonstrated in Example 6 and the conjugate summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose the conjugate, expand the numerator, collect like surds and identify two signed coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Form reciprocal sums, combine conjugate fractions and cancel cross terms; part d extends these routine steps to algebraic radicands.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates a value plus its reciprocal. Parts a and b rationalise a binomial reciprocal directly; parts c and d combine reciprocal fractions using conjugate products. The binomial rationalisation skill is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate and use the difference of squares; expand and simplify surd expressions with exact arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form reciprocal sums, combine conjugate fractions and cancel cross terms; part d extends these routine steps to algebraic radicands.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught conjugate method to algebraic radicands, simplify the denominator to h and recognise the exceptional h=0 case.

questions.mappingNote: The denominator contains two surd terms with algebraic radicands, so binomial surd rationalisation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate, then simplify the denominator using the difference of squares, as in Key Ideas 11–12 and Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught conjugate method to algebraic radicands, simplify the denominator to h and recognise the exceptional h=0 case.

classification.difficultyReason: The required identity supplies the rationalised target; students apply the taught conjugate method, substitute the approximation and compare accuracy.

questions.mappingNote: Part b directly assesses rationalising a binomial surd denominator, then applies the equivalent expression to compare approximation accuracy.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate and simplify the denominator using the difference of squares, as in Example 6 and the conjugates explanation.
